title: Release Engineering
subtitle: Make the released binary and configuration reproducible and traceable
summary: Release engineering makes delivery a repeatable engineering process from source revision to running service. Hermetic builds control their tools and dependencies so an older version can be rebuilt without accidentally incorporating today’s environment. Release branches and selected fixes identify the intended changes, but the resulting combination must still pass tests. Packaging gives artifacts stable identities and an audit trail that helps responders understand what is running. Deployment then promotes those artifacts at a pace suited to the service’s risk, with canaries and staged expansion where appropriate. Configuration deserves the same care as binaries: its packaging and version relationship determine whether a deployment can be reconstructed. Self-service tools and explicit policies let teams release frequently while keeping these controls consistent.

concepts.title: Hermetic builds
concepts.body: A hermetic build obtains its inputs from declared, controlled sources instead of whatever tools or libraries happen to be installed on a machine. Versioning build tools as well as source code makes rebuilding an older release meaningful. Reproducibility reduces uncertainty when investigating failures: a rebuild for one fix should not silently introduce an unrelated compiler or dependency change.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A repair to last month’s release uses its recorded compiler and dependencies plus the selected source fix.

concepts.title: Release contents must be tested together
concepts.body: Google’s workflow creates a release branch at a known revision and selectively adds fixes already submitted to mainline. This controls which changes enter the release, but the resulting branch may be a combination never tested on mainline. Running release tests on that exact combination establishes evidence about what will ship and records an audit trail of its validation.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: Two individually passing cherry-picks are tested together on the release branch before packaging.

concepts.title: Artifact identity and staged deployment
concepts.body: A package identifies the actual built contents, while labels can indicate its place in the release workflow. Deployments should reference the intended version and preserve a trace from source through testing to production. Canarying and progressive rollout expose changes to limited traffic first; expansion pace depends on risk and the observations needed to find problems, rather than a universal release schedule.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A canary and the wider rollout use the same package hash instead of rebuilding between stages.

concepts.title: Configuration is part of the release
concepts.body: Configuration can change service behavior as profoundly as a binary. Keeping it reviewed and versioned makes changes intentional, but teams must choose how it is distributed. Bundling configuration with binaries simplifies matching; separate packages permit independent changes; dynamic stores support runtime updates. Each choice needs a clear way to identify the running configuration and its compatibility with the binary.
concepts.example: Teaching extension: A flag-only repair deploys a new versioned configuration package without rebuilding the executable.

misconceptions.claim: If every change passed mainline tests, a cherry-picked release needs no retest.
misconceptions.correction: The assembled release branch is a distinct combination and must be validated as shipped.

misconceptions.claim: A configuration change is too small to need release discipline.
misconceptions.correction: Configuration changes behavior and can create incompatible or untraceable production states.

scenario.title: Promote a reproducible release
scenario.context: A library change passes tests but has two dependency versions in different build environments. The team can promote one immutable artifact through stages or rebuild separately in production.

options.label: Build once and promote the artifact
options.benefit: The tested bits remain the bits deployed, making rollback clearer.
options.cost: The pipeline must preserve configuration separation.
options.consequence: The canary uses the same artifact and is widened only after health checks.

options.label: Rebuild at each environment
options.benefit: Environment-specific builds can adapt to local requirements.
options.cost: Drift can make a production failure impossible to reproduce.
options.consequence: The production rebuild works but creates a second debugging dimension.

scenario.debrief: Immutable promotion preserves the tested artifact; rebuilding per environment is acceptable only when the resulting drift is explicit and testable.

quiz.question: Which input most directly breaks build hermeticity?
options: An undeclared library from the developer’s laptop
quiz.explanation: An undeclared local dependency makes the result depend on the machine’s environment.

quiz.question: Why retest a release branch after cherry-picking fixes?
options: Its combined contents may never have existed on mainline
Cherry-picking always changes the programming language
quiz.explanation: The release needs evidence about its own exact code combination.

quiz.question: A flag needs changing without rebuilding the binary. Which model supports this while retaining traceability?
options: Edit an unrecorded file on every host
Release a separately versioned configuration package
Replace the package hash with a mutable filename only
quiz.explanation: Separate configuration packaging allows independent changes with a recorded identity.

exercise.title: Trace one release end to end
exercise.prompt: Describe how an emergency source fix becomes a tested package, then a canary, then a wider release. Include the configuration version.
